steps.title: Per-IP failures from the raw log
steps.do: Full command: grep 'Failed password' auth-jump01.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn  Typed in two parts. In the Terminal window type grep 'Failed password' auth-jump01.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' (grep Failed password, then the log name, piped to awk, the fourth field from the end, because invalid user lines are longer so a fixed field would grab the wrong word). Continue on the same line with  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn (leading space), so each IP gets a count, biggest first. Press Return. Read the counts under the prompt: 18 203.0.113.45, 14 198.51.100.23, 9 192.0.2.77, 7 198.51.100.140, 3 for the ten-dot address (10.20.4.11), 2 192.0.2.200. Method to say: $(NF-3) when lines differ in word count (invalid user lines add words); a fixed field only when every line has the same shape. Counting from the raw log, not the sheet, means an import slip would show. Check those six against D3:D8 in the pivot, 18, 14, 9, 7, 3, 2: all match.

steps.title: Epilogue
steps.do: Epilogue: no clicks. Keep the pivot on screen and talk through six topics in order, three short lines each. 1. What was done start to finish: Terminal counts first, then the pivot, then each IP's raw rows. 2. The evidence behind the Block IPs: 203.0.113.45 (18 failures) and 198.51.100.23 (14), no success on either; the block is temporary, 24h here. 3. Why the Watch IPs got account actions: 192.0.2.77 and 198.51.100.140 got in after failures (svc_backup, jsmith). 4. How the Terminal checks matched the sheet: 53 against the grep count, 59 rows against the 59 log lines. 5. What the two files contain and where they are: final output 1.xlsx and final output 2.docx in Documents, Project. 6. What you would do next with more time: more nights of logs, a known office or VPN range check, a daily counting script.
say: "Step 35: I counted in Terminal first, so the sheet had numbers to hit."
"Then the pivot, which counts every IP and event, sorted riskiest first."
"I read each IP's raw rows before choosing, since a count doesn't show who got in."
"For 203.0.113.45 and 198.51.100.23, 18 and 14 failures, no success on either."
"On block length, fail2ban's default is ten minutes, though plenty of admins raise it to a day."
"The block is temporary, 24h here, easy to undo if an address is shared."
"The easy miss is a success after failures. For 192.0.2.77 and 198.51.100.140, svc_backup and jsmith both got in."
"An address that got in is an account problem first, so those got account checks."
"Blocking them could lock out a shared office and leave a stolen password working."
"The pivot's grand total of 53 matched the grep count, and 59 rows matched the 59 log lines."
"The tricky part was the log. Lines vary in length, so a fixed awk field grabs the wrong word."
"After the export I recounted failures per IP from the raw log, and they matched column D, logins too."
"The files are in Documents, Project. The first file, final output 1, is the sheet as .xlsx, raw rows on Sheet1 and the pivot on Pivot Table 1."
"The second file, final output 2, is the note as .docx, with the 20 Oct heading, the table, and one action line per decision word."
"I opened both after downloading, and the table is unlinked, so it won't drift."
"With more time I'd pull more nights of logs, to see if these addresses come back."
"I'd check whether any belong to a known office or VPN range before a longer block."
"I'd save the Terminal counts as a script, so the cross-check runs every morning."
